\section{Motivation}
\label{sec:introduction:motivation}
Language models utilize information in tables, text, and images to make predictions and respond to queries. 
However, the required information is often incomplete or distributed across sources. A table may list people without identifying their occupations. A classification task may introduce labels absent from its initial training examples. A question may require facts from several passages or a relationship expressed jointly by text and images. 
Hence, selecting relevant evidences and preserving their connections are therefore crucial real-world problems.

In this thesis, we study how explicit knowledge structures can support evidence selection for language model reasoning.

Knowledge graphs provide descriptions absent from a table. Task graphs maintain associations between keywords and classification labels. Evidence graphs connect facts across passages, while query graphs specify the relationships needed to answer a multimodal question. We develop methods that use these relationships to retrieve evidence and control how it is processed.

% 这里同样，应该有一个研究主线，再从主线引出我们的具体研究问题
Our first problem is column type annotation. A column of people accompanied by birth and death dates may lack the information needed to identify their common occupation. Linking the names to a knowledge graph can supply that information, but the graph may assign several valid types to each person. These types may also differ from the annotation vocabulary. We propose KGLink to select relevant graph descriptions and learn their correspondence to the target labels~\cite{kglink-publication}.

% 第二个问题应该顺承第一个研究问题，也要follow主线
Our second problem is dynamic few-shot text classification. New labels arrive over successive rounds, with only a few examples for each class. A fixed retrieval budget does not determine which labels are relevant to the current text, and uniformly indexing observed words can retain incidental associations. We propose GORAG to maintain weighted keyword--label relations and retrieve candidate labels by connecting query keywords~\cite{gorag-paper}.

% 第三个和第四个问题既可以是串行关系，也可以是并行的，都顺承于第二个研究问题
Our third problem is evidence retrieval for textual question answering and generation. Individually relevant passages can repeat facts or leave their connections implicit. A short path between query anchors can also omit information needed for a summary. We propose AGRAG to select a connected subgraph using query-dependent node influence and semantic edge costs. Hybrid passage retrieval supplies context beyond the selected graph~\cite{agrag-paper}.

Our fourth problem is multimodal question answering. A relation stated directly in a question may correspond to several relations in the evidence, and a graph constructed before seeing the query can omit relevant visual details. We propose MGRAG to build query-specific evidence graphs and match query relations to semantic paths. Graph features also guide the recomputation of cached model states when the retrieved content is used for answering~\cite{mgrag-paper}.

These problems lead to a common research question. How can explicit relationships improve the selection and processing of evidence for language models? We investigate external knowledge selection, online index maintenance, connected textual retrieval, and semantic matching over multimodal evidence.

\section{Motivation}
\label{sec:introduction:motivation}
Language models utilize information in tables, text, and images to make predictions and respond to queries. 
However, the required information is often incomplete or distributed across sources. A table may list people without identifying their occupations. A classification task may introduce labels absent from its initial training examples. A question may require facts from several passages or a relationship expressed jointly by text and images. 
Hence, selecting relevant evidence and preserving its connections are crucial real-world problems.

The usefulness of external information depends on how it relates to the current task. A person's occupation can help identify a table column, while a keyword's association with a label can help classify a text. For question answering, several facts may need to be connected before they can support an answer. Explicit knowledge structures represent these relationships and make them available when selecting information for a language model. This motivates our study of structural augmentation, from enriching model representations with existing knowledge graphs to constructing task-related graphs for retrieval and reasoning.

We first investigate how an existing knowledge graph can supply information missing from a model's input. In column type annotation, a column of people accompanied by birth and death dates may lack the information needed to identify their common occupation. Linking the names to a knowledge graph can supply that information, but the graph may assign several valid types to each person. These types may also differ from the annotation vocabulary. We propose KGLink to select relevant graph descriptions and integrate them with a pre-trained table encoder. Through supervised fine-tuning, the encoder learns their correspondence to the target labels~\cite{kglink-publication}.

KGLink's use of external knowledge depends on the coverage of the existing graph and the labeled data available for fine-tuning. When a suitable graph is unavailable or new labels arrive with few examples, the system needs another way to obtain and use knowledge. We explore using a large language model's semantic capabilities with a graph constructed from task data. We propose GORAG for dynamic few-shot text classification. GORAG constructs weighted keyword--label relations, retrieves candidate labels by connecting query keywords, and updates the graph as new labels and texts arrive~\cite{gorag-paper}. The system incorporates new information through index updates without requiring a predefined knowledge graph or model fine-tuning.

Building a graph from task data extends structural augmentation to settings without a predefined knowledge graph. For question answering and generation, however, retrieving candidate labels is no longer sufficient. The model needs facts that jointly support an answer, and a summary can require several complementary information items. Individually relevant passages can repeat facts or leave their connections implicit, while a short path between query anchors can omit required details. We propose AGRAG to construct a graph from the text corpus and select a connected evidence subgraph using query-dependent node influence and semantic edge costs. Subgraph expansion and hybrid passage retrieval supply additional facts and context for answer generation~\cite{agrag-paper}.

Multimodal question answering introduces a further requirement for task-related graph construction and retrieval. Relevant facts can be distributed across text and images, and the visual details needed from an image depend on the question. A relation stated directly in that question may also correspond to several relations in the evidence. We propose MGRAG to build query-specific evidence graphs and match query relations to semantic paths~\cite{mgrag-paper}. Query-aware construction selects relevant facts, while path matching checks their correspondence to the requested relationships. The selected structure also guides the recomputation of cached model states when the evidence is processed for answering.

In this thesis, we study how explicit knowledge structures can help language models obtain and use the evidence required by a task. We begin with knowledge-enriched representation learning, then reduce the dependence on existing knowledge graphs and task-specific fine-tuning through graph-based retrieval. We further investigate connected textual evidence and query-aware multimodal matching as two extensions to more complex answer requirements.

KGLink learns column labels from annotated tables and retrieves descriptions from an external graph. GORAG initializes its index from labeled examples and updates it using subsequent predictions. AGRAG and MGRAG construct their evidence graphs from source documents.

\subsection{Reasoning through task-specific evidence}

We evaluate the structural operations through annotation accuracy and F1, classification accuracy across label rounds, task-specific answer measures, and context-processing costs.

The four studies have separate implementations and evaluations. They address successive problems in obtaining external knowledge, maintaining an index, selecting connected text, and matching multimodal evidence.

We also examine information preservation in hyper-relational knowledge graphs. This study distinguishes qualifier capture from graph reception and develops FormerGNN to combine them. It appears in the background chapter and provides a basis for analyzing information lost during graph transformation.

\subsection{The evidence interface as a design choice}
The available information determines each retrieval decision. KGLink uses table content and linked descriptions, with a masked type position at inference. GORAG uses the support examples and index updates available before the current prediction. AGRAG selects from a fixed corpus graph for each query. MGRAG progressively extracts query-related facts from ranked multimodal chunks.

\subsection{RQ2: Evidence maintenance under evolving labels}
The second question asks how a retrieval index can maintain task-specific relationships and select relevant labels as a few-shot classification problem evolves. The input includes the examples and labels available at the current round, an existing graph index, and an unseen text. The output is a label prediction and the prescribed index update for subsequent processing.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion:findings}
In this thesis, we developed four methods that use explicit knowledge structures to select and process evidence for language models. The methods address missing table context, evolving classification labels, connected textual evidence, and semantic correspondence across multimodal sources.

We proposed KGLink to enrich column representations with graph descriptions and learn their correspondence to annotation labels. Cross-column filtering selects relevant descriptions, and contextual type-representation training helps the encoder use them. The model also retains a table-encoding pathway for columns without KG evidence.

We proposed GORAG to maintain a keyword--label graph for dynamic few-shot classification. Connected retrieval produces a candidate set for each query, while online insertion expands the index after prediction. The ablations show the benefit of these updates, with dataset-dependent effects as support and label sets grow.

We proposed AGRAG to select connected textual evidence using node influence and semantic edge costs. Expanding the initial tree supplies additional answer components, while hybrid passages retain context beyond the selected graph. The ablations show how these choices affect answer coverage and faithfulness.

We proposed MGRAG to construct query-specific multimodal graphs and match query relations to semantic paths. Graph-aware recomputation extends the use of the retrieved structure to context processing. The experiments show improved answer quality, with runtime effects that depend on the retrieval pipeline.

The accompanying hyper-relational knowledge-graph study examined how structural representations preserve fact information. Its qualifier-capture and graph-reception perspectives help explain why the form of a representation matters. Across the thesis, the common design question is which relationships must remain explicit for the downstream task.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion:findings}
In this thesis, we investigated how explicit knowledge structures support language-model prediction and reasoning. Our research progressed from enrichment with an existing knowledge graph to graph construction from task data and retrieval without model fine-tuning. We further studied answers requiring connected textual facts or relationships distributed across text and images.

We first proposed KGLink to enrich column representations with external graph descriptions. Cross-column filtering selects relevant descriptions, and contextual type-representation training learns their correspondence to annotation labels. The trained encoder also predicts from table values when KG evidence is unavailable.

To remove the dependence on existing knowledge graphs and model fine-tuning, we proposed GORAG for dynamic few-shot classification. GORAG constructs a keyword--label graph from task data and retrieves candidate classes for a large language model. Online insertion incorporates newly observed vocabulary without updating model parameters. Experiments show the benefit of connected retrieval and online updates as labels accumulate.

We then studied the evidence requirements of question answering and generation. AGRAG constructs a graph from a text corpus and selects connected facts using query-dependent node influence and semantic edge costs. Expanding the initial tree supplies additional answer components, while hybrid passages retain context beyond the selected graph. The ablations show how these evidence channels contribute to information coverage and answer faithfulness.

For multimodal question answering, we proposed MGRAG to construct query-specific graphs and match requested relations to semantic paths. Graph-aware recomputation extends the use of structure to context processing. The experiments relate answer quality to query-aware extraction and matching, and measure cache reuse quality and cost.

Our hyper-relational knowledge-graph study examined how graph transformations preserve fact information. Qualifier capture and graph reception explain how the representation and the model jointly determine which relationships remain available for prediction.

Language models depend on the evidence supplied to their prediction and generation processes. Tables can omit information needed for semantic annotation, classification labels can evolve under limited supervision, and answers can require relationships distributed across textual and visual sources. This thesis investigates how explicit knowledge structures can organize and select evidence for these settings.

The thesis develops four methods for structural augmentation. KGLink integrates knowledge graphs with a pre-trained language model to enrich column representations and bridge differences between graph types and annotation labels. GORAG supports dynamic few-shot classification through connected label retrieval and an online graph index that evolves with the task. AGRAG selects connected textual evidence by combining query-dependent node influence, semantic edge costs, and hybrid passage retrieval. MGRAG constructs query-specific multimodal graphs, matches query relations to semantic paths, and uses graph structure to guide the reuse and recomputation of cached model states.

Experiments across table annotation, dynamic classification, textual generation, and multimodal question answering show improved effectiveness over established baselines and efficiency gains in graph indexing and context processing. Ablation studies verify the contributions of the structural components. A related study of hyper-relational knowledge graphs examines information preservation. These studies demonstrate how explicit relationships improve evidence representation, retrieval, and computation for language models.

Language models utilize external information to make predictions and answer questions when their inputs lack the required knowledge. Explicit knowledge structures can expose relationships that help select and use this information. However, augmentation with an existing knowledge graph depends on its coverage, and supervised model adaptation requires labeled data and fine-tuning. This thesis investigates structural augmentation from knowledge-enriched representation learning to task-related graph retrieval and reasoning.

We first propose KGLink to enrich column representations with knowledge-graph descriptions and learn their correspondence to annotation labels. To remove the dependence on a predefined knowledge graph and task-specific fine-tuning, we propose GORAG to construct and update a task graph for dynamic few-shot classification. Connected retrieval supplies candidate labels to a large language model. We further study evidence requirements beyond classification. AGRAG selects connected textual facts and supporting passages for question answering and generation. MGRAG constructs query-specific multimodal graphs, matches query relations to semantic paths, and uses graph structure to guide the reuse and recomputation of cached model states.

Experiments across these tasks show improvements in prediction and answer quality, with efficiency gains in graph indexing and context processing. Ablation studies examine the contributions of the structural components. A related study of hyper-relational knowledge graphs analyzes information preservation under graph transformations.
